title: Good Faith Exam Med Spa Requirements: Who, When and How Often (2026)
summary: Good faith exam med spa requirements explained: who can perform one, when a repeat is due, and how to track renewals so no patient is treated uncovered.
body_markdown:
## What Is a Good Faith Exam at a Med Spa?


A good faith exam is a medical evaluation by a licensed prescriber that happens before a patient receives a prescription-based treatment. It establishes that the treatment is medically appropriate for this person, and it gives the clinic a dated record showing a qualified provider made that call. The term is industry shorthand. Statutes rarely use the phrase itself.


California is a good example. There the expectation comes from[Business and Professions Code section 2242](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=2242) , which treats prescribing or furnishing dangerous drugs without an appropriate prior examination and medical indication as unprofessional conduct. Neurotoxin, many fillers with lidocaine, and most IV formulations land in that category. Other states build the same idea out of nurse practice acts, physician delegation rules or med spa statutes.


What the exam is not matters just as much. A sales consultation, a photo review by an aesthetician and a patient filling out a form are all useful, and none of them is the exam. The prescriber has to evaluate the patient and own the decision.


## Who Can Perform a Good Faith Exam?


In most states a physician, a physician assistant or a nurse practitioner performs the exam, working inside their scope of practice and any supervision or collaboration agreement. The[American Med Spa Association](https://americanmedspa.org/blog/what-is-required-of-a-medical-spas-good-faith-exams) describes the same group and notes that registered nurses can assist, for example by collecting history, but the prescriber has to review the findings and generate the plan.


The trap is hiring a nurse practitioner and assuming the box is checked. Whether that provider may exam patients independently, and whether they may do it for patients of a clinic they do not work in, depends on your state and on the paperwork you have with your medical director. A founder staffing a new clinic or a mobile service should settle this before the first booking goes live.


Standing orders are a separate question. A completed exam does not by itself authorize a specific treatment in states that require a patient-specific order, which our guide to[standing orders and patient-specific orders](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-standing-orders-patient-specific-orders-explained) walks through.


## How Often Is a Good Faith Exam Required?


There is rarely a statutory interval, so the schedule is a policy your medical director sets. The working industry default is an exam before the first treatment, a renewal about every twelve months, and an earlier exam whenever the clinical picture changes. ByrdAdatto's guidance, published through AmSpa, calls annual renewal a good rule of thumb for exactly this reason: no statute tells you otherwise, so a clean annual cycle is easy to defend.


The table below shows how that default usually plays out. Treat it as a draft for your medical director, because your state may be stricter.


Situation New exam needed? Why


New patient, first prescription treatment Yes, before treatment No prescriber has evaluated this patient yet


Repeat neurotoxin every 12 weeks, nothing changed No, until the annual renewal The exam on file still supports the same treatment


Neurotoxin patient now wants filler or an IV drip Yes A new treatment category is a new clinical decision


New medication, pregnancy or diagnosis Yes, before the next visit The health picture the exam relied on has changed


Exam older than your renewal window Yes Your policy, not the calendar on the patient's side, expired it


Some states say less than this and some say more. Pabau's guide, for instance, covers only four states and tells readers to check their board for the rest. Do the same, and write the answer into your clinic policy so every staff member applies it the same way.


## Can a Good Faith Exam Be Done by Telehealth?


In many states, yes. The exam can be performed remotely when it meets the standard of care and the state's telehealth rules, which often include documenting that the patient consented to a remote visit. California's telehealth statute,[section 2290.5](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=2290.5) , is one example of that consent requirement. Other states are stricter and want live video, and a few have narrower rules for certain drugs.


This is why many clinics use a telehealth exam partner instead of hiring a prescriber for it. Decoda Health integrates with[Spakinect](https://decodahealth.com/partnerships/spakinect) and[Qualiphy](https://decodahealth.com/partnerships/qualiphy) for partner exams. Ask whichever partner you consider two things: which states they cover, and what format they use in yours. A prospect evaluating an IV startup in the Midwest put it plainly: she wanted the exam routed through the EMR so her per diem nurses never had to ask whether a patient was cleared.


## What Does the Exam Have to Include?


At a minimum the exam documents the patient's medical history, current medications, allergies, relevant conditions such as pregnancy, and the prescriber's assessment that the planned treatment is appropriate. When the exam is physical, it also records what was examined. The record should name the examining provider and carry a date.


Think about what you would have to produce if a board or insurer asked. You would need the questionnaire the patient completed, the prescriber's conclusion, the date, and the link between that exam and the treatment delivered. Our guide to[med spa consent forms](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-consent-forms) covers the signature side of that record. For GLP-1, testosterone and peptide programs the history is longer, and the[screening intake guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/glp1-trt-peptide-patient-screening-intake) lists what to collect.


## Why Do Clinics Treat Patients Without Valid Coverage?


Almost never out of defiance. Operators who describe the problem to us say the exam gets requested late, the renewal date lives in someone's head or a spreadsheet, and the front desk discovers the gap with the patient already in the chair. Each of those is a process failure, and each is fixable.


A typical failure looks like this. A patient books a filler visit three weeks out. Her exam from last November quietly expired in the meantime. Nobody checks, she arrives, and now the clinic has three options, all bad: reschedule a patient who took time off, treat anyway, or squeeze in a same-day exam. The fix is to check coverage when the booking is made, not when the patient shows up.


Mobile services make this sharper. A nurse who drives to a home cannot call the front desk to ask about paperwork mid-visit, so coverage has to be settled before the route is planned. Our[mobile IV booking setup guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/mobile-iv-booking-setup-guide) shows how to build that gate into scheduling.


## How Should You Track Renewals Without a Spreadsheet?


Track the exam date per patient, compute the expiry from your renewal window, and surface anything expiring before the appointment, not on the day. Four habits do most of the work:


- **Request the exam at booking.** A patient who books online should be sent the exam request in the same confirmation, with the intake questions, instead of a week later.
- **Check coverage against the treatment.** An exam covering neurotoxin does not necessarily cover an IV drip. The check has to look at what is being booked.
- **Flag expiry ahead of the visit.** Run a weekly list of appointments in the next fourteen days whose exams will have lapsed by then, and work it before reminders go out.
- **Show status where the front desk works.** A green, expiring or missing indicator on the check-in screen beats a login to a separate portal.


If you still track this by hand, start with a single sheet: patient, exam date, exam type, expiry, treatments covered. It will not scale past a few hundred patients, but it will show you how often the date slips.

## What Do New Laws Mean for Good Faith Exams?


They push the same direction: more documentation, tied to the chart, produced on request. Several states have tightened med spa oversight recently, and the practical effect is that a physician-directed, individualized record is expected for every patient. Our summary of[new med spa laws](https://decodahealth.com/blog/new-med-spa-laws) covers the California changes, and the[registration and licensure](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-registration-and-licensure) guide covers what your state asks at the business level.


Check your state medical and nursing boards each year, and ask your attorney to review the written policy once. The[American Med Spa Association](https://www.americanmedspa.org/) tracks state changes and is a reasonable place for an owner to start.


## Final Thoughts on Good Faith Exam Requirements


Pick the schedule with your medical director, write it down in one page, and move the check to the moment of booking. That single change turns the exam from something staff remember into something the schedule enforces. ## Frequently Asked Questions


What is a good faith exam at a med spa?


A good faith exam is a medical evaluation by a licensed prescriber before a patient receives a prescription-based treatment such as neurotoxin, filler or an IV formulation. It reviews history, medications and allergies, and it documents that the treatment is medically appropriate for that patient. It is not a sales consultation or an intake chat with the front desk.


How often is a good faith exam required?


Most state rules do not set a fixed interval, so clinics follow a policy written with their medical director and attorney. The common default is one exam before the first treatment and a fresh one about every twelve months, plus an earlier exam when the patient starts a new treatment category or their health changes. Confirm the schedule against your own state board.


Who is allowed to perform a good faith exam?


Generally a physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner acting within their state scope of practice. Registered nurses and aestheticians usually cannot complete the exam on their own, although they may gather history for the prescriber to review. Rules differ by state, so check your medical and nursing board before assigning the task to anyone.


Can a good faith exam be done by telehealth?


In many states yes, provided the exam meets the standard of care and the telehealth rules of that state, which often include documented patient consent. Some states expect a live video visit and others accept a reviewed questionnaire. Ask your medical director which format your state accepts before you rely on a remote exam partner.


Do you need a new good faith exam for every appointment?


No. A patient returning for the same treatment with an unchanged health picture is usually covered by the exam on file. A new exam is due when the exam expires under your policy, when the patient starts a different category of treatment, or when something clinical changes, such as a new medication, pregnancy or diagnosis.


What happens if a med spa treats a patient without a valid good faith exam?


The clinic and the prescriber are exposed to board discipline, and the treating staff may be acting outside their scope. Penalties differ by state and can include fines and license action. The practical fix is to make coverage visible before the visit, so the front desk never has to decide at check-in whether a patient can be treated.
